Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BANGKOK, Thailand (CNN) -- Thailand's military has denied abusing refugee boat-people from Myanmar after claims some were whipped on a tourist beach and hundreds more left dead or missing after being towed at to sea without food and water. Photograph released by Thai navy showing a group of illegal immigrants captured on December 12. Photos showing refugees being made to lie face down on a popular beach and media reports claiming refugees been deliberately lost at sea have sparked concerns for their safety. The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees says it is "concerned" about the fate of the Muslim ethnic minority Rohingya people, who have fled from Myanmar's border with Bangladesh. The agency says it has written a formal note to the Thai Ministry of Foreign Affairs asking for clarification of what is happening. CNN spoke to one Australian tourist, who declined to be named for fear of being barred from Thailand, who says boat-people were "whipped" by Thai guards on popular diving resort island in the Similan Archipelago last month. Local media also report claims by Rohingya survivors that the Thai military have been detaining hundreds of them an island called Koh Sai Daeng before towing them back out into open water without supplies. The survivors say hundreds of them drowned and only the lucky ones made it to the Indian Andaman Islands or Indonesia's Aceh province. The Thai Navy denies knowledge of the incident. Rear Admiral Naris Pratumsuwan told CNN "as a normal practice, if Navy finds illegal immigrants, we will hand them over to related authorities, e.g. police or immigration police." He said he had not received any information on an island where migrants are being detained. There were reports of another boatload of 46 Rohingya detained by the Thai military Friday, but there was no official confirmation. The Rohingya have been fleeing persecution of the hard-line military regime in Myanmar, formerly Burma, for years and often seek refuge in Malaysia. Boat loads of Rohingya arriving in Thailand is nothing new, but non-governmental organizations are increasingly worried about what they say is an apparent change of government policy. They say the army's Internal Security Operations Command is forcing the Rohingya out to sea rather than deporting them overland back to Myanmar. "The Thai government is taking highly vulnerable people and risking their lives for political gain," says Refugee International's Sean Garcia says. "It should be engaging the Burmese government on improving conditions at home for the Rohingya if it wants to stem these flows. "The Rohingya will continue to make the journey because they have no hope for a better life in Burma. Pushing them back out to sea is not an effective deterrent it just jeopardizes lives."

**BANGKOK, Thailand (CNN) —** Thailand’s military has denied abusing boat people from Myanmar following allegations that some were whipped on a tourist beach and that hundreds of others were left dead or missing after being towed out to sea without food or water.

A photograph released by the Thai Navy shows a group of illegal immigrants captured on December 12.

Images of refugees being forced to lie face down on a popular beach, along with media reports alleging that refugees were deliberately abandoned at sea, have raised concerns about their safety.

The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees says it is “concerned” about the fate of the Rohingya, a Muslim ethnic minority who have fled Myanmar’s border region with Bangladesh. The agency says it has sent a formal note to the Thai Ministry of Foreign Affairs seeking clarification about the situation.

CNN spoke with an Australian tourist who declined to be named for fear of being barred from Thailand. The tourist said boat people were “whipped” by Thai guards last month on a popular diving-resort island in the Similan Archipelago.

Local media have also reported claims by Rohingya survivors that the Thai military detained hundreds of them on an island called Koh Sai Daeng before towing them back into open water without supplies. The survivors said hundreds drowned and that only the fortunate reached India’s Andaman Islands or Indonesia’s Aceh province.

The Thai Navy has denied any knowledge of the incident. Rear Admiral Naris Pratumsuwan told CNN, “As a normal practice, if the Navy finds illegal immigrants, we will hand them over to the relevant authorities, e.g., the police or immigration police.” He said he had received no information about an island where migrants were allegedly being detained.

There were also reports that another boat carrying 46 Rohingya was detained by the Thai military on Friday, but there was no official confirmation.

For years, the Rohingya have been fleeing persecution by the hard-line military regime in Myanmar, formerly known as Burma, and often seek refuge in Malaysia. While boatloads of Rohingya arriving in Thailand are nothing new, nongovernmental organizations are increasingly concerned about what they describe as an apparent shift in government policy.

They allege that the army’s Internal Security Operations Command is forcing the Rohingya back out to sea rather than deporting them overland to Myanmar.

“The Thai government is taking highly vulnerable people and risking their lives for political gain,” said Sean Garcia of Refugees International. “It should be engaging the Burmese government on improving conditions at home for the Rohingya if it wants to stem these flows.

“The Rohingya will continue to make the journey because they have no hope for a better life in Burma. Pushing them back out to sea is not an effective deterrent; it just jeopardizes lives.”

**Thailand accused of abusing Rohingya migrants, abandoning boats at sea**

**Bangkok, Thailand** — Thailand’s military is facing allegations that security forces detained and abused Rohingya refugees before forcing hundreds of migrants back to sea in boats with little or no food and water.

Survivors and human rights groups say migrants arriving on Thailand’s southern coast were taken into military custody, beaten and held outdoors before being placed on vessels that were towed into international waters and abandoned.

Some survivors reportedly spent days drifting in overcrowded boats. Others were later rescued near Indonesia and India, according to rights organizations and regional authorities. The total number of deaths remains unclear, and the accounts have not all been independently verified.

Human rights advocates have called for an independent investigation, warning that forcibly returning migrants to dangerous conditions could violate international law.

Thai officials have denied systematically mistreating the Rohingya, saying authorities act to protect the country’s borders and combat human-smuggling networks. The military has previously said any misconduct by individual personnel would be investigated.

The Rohingya are a predominantly Muslim minority from Myanmar who have long faced restrictions, discrimination and violence. Many have attempted dangerous sea journeys toward Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia.

The allegations are renewing pressure on Southeast Asian governments to coordinate humanitarian rescues and ensure migrants are not pushed back into life-threatening conditions.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a detailed article on the UNHCR’s concerns over Thailand’s treatment of Rohingya boat people fleeing persecution in Myanmar, including military denials and survivor accounts.
counterfactuals.output:
# UNHCR Raises Alarm Over Thailand’s Treatment of Rohingya Boat People

Thailand’s handling of Rohingya refugees arriving by sea has repeatedly drawn concern from the United Nations refugee agency amid allegations that Thai security forces detained, abused and expelled boat people without properly assessing their need for protection.

The most serious accusations emerged during the large-scale maritime movements of 2008 and 2009, when survivors said Thai personnel intercepted Rohingya boats in the Andaman Sea, held passengers in military custody and then towed some vessels back into international waters with inadequate food, water or fuel. Thai military officials denied deliberately endangering the migrants and maintained that security forces had provided humanitarian assistance or acted under procedures intended to prevent illegal entry and smuggling.

The conflicting accounts placed Thailand at the center of an early regional debate over maritime “pushbacks”—the interception and removal of asylum seekers without allowing them meaningful access to refugee-status procedures.

## A persecuted minority fleeing Myanmar

The Rohingya are a predominantly Muslim ethnic minority from Myanmar’s western Rakhine State. Myanmar’s 1982 citizenship law excluded most Rohingya from full citizenship, leaving generations effectively stateless. They have faced severe restrictions on movement, education, employment, marriage and access to health care, along with recurring violence and military operations.

Long before the Myanmar military’s mass campaign in 2017 drove more than 700,000 Rohingya into Bangladesh, thousands were already attempting dangerous voyages across the Bay of Bengal and Andaman Sea. Many hoped to reach Malaysia, where they believed jobs and established Rohingya communities offered a chance of survival.

The journeys were often organized by smugglers and undertaken in overcrowded, unseaworthy boats. Passengers commonly carried little food or water and were vulnerable to storms, extortion, trafficking and abuse.

## Reports of interception and expulsion

In late 2008 and early 2009, reports began circulating that Thai authorities had intercepted several vessels near the country’s Andaman coast. Journalists and human-rights organizations published photographs and testimony indicating that large groups of Rohingya men had been detained on beaches or offshore islands under military supervision.

Survivors later rescued near India’s Andaman and Nicobar Islands and in Indonesia said Thai forces had forced them onto boats and towed them far out to sea. Some alleged that engines had been removed or disabled and that only limited food and water had been left aboard before the tow lines were cut.

According to survivor accounts collected by journalists, humanitarian groups and Indonesian officials, passengers drifted for days or weeks. Some said people died from dehydration, starvation or exposure and that bodies were put overboard. Others described desperate attempts to collect rainwater or divide the small amount of food remaining.

Several survivors also alleged that they had been beaten while in Thai custody, had their hands bound or were made to lie face down for long periods. Because many were interviewed only after traumatic voyages and because access to the original detention sites was restricted, some details varied. Nevertheless, the accounts shared a central allegation: the passengers had been removed from Thai territory and left at sea in conditions that placed their lives in danger.

## UNHCR seeks access and explanations

The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, or UNHCR, expressed concern about the reports and sought access to Rohingya detained by Thailand. The agency wanted to determine who the passengers were, whether any wished to seek asylum and whether they were at risk of being returned to persecution.

UNHCR stressed that people intercepted at sea must be treated humanely and that states should respect the principle of **non-refoulement**. That principle prohibits returning a person to a country or territory where they face persecution, torture or other serious harm.

Thailand is not a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention or its 1967 Protocol and does not have a comprehensive asylum system equivalent to those in many convention states. UNHCR and human-rights organizations have nonetheless argued that the prohibition on refoulement is a broader obligation under customary international law and other human-rights treaties binding on Thailand.

The agency’s concerns extended beyond the question of formal refugee status. Maritime law and basic humanitarian standards require authorities to protect life at sea. Sending an unseaworthy or poorly supplied boat away from shore, if established, could violate those duties regardless of the passengers’ immigration status.

UNHCR therefore called for transparency, access to detainees and a full investigation into what had happened to the intercepted boats. It also urged Thai authorities to distinguish among refugees, trafficking victims and other migrants rather than treating every arrival solely as an illegal-entry case.

## Thai military rejects allegations

Thai military officials denied that their personnel had intentionally abandoned Rohingya at sea. They said the armed forces had given passengers food, water or medical assistance and disputed allegations of systematic beating or mistreatment.

Some officials described Thailand’s approach as “helping on” the boats rather than pushing them back. Under that account, authorities repaired or resupplied vessels and allowed passengers to continue toward their stated destinations rather than detaining them indefinitely in Thailand.

The military also argued that the Andaman coast faced organized smuggling operations and that some boats were part of networks transporting undocumented migrants toward Malaysia. Officials said border and maritime forces were responsible for protecting national security and enforcing immigration law.

Thailand’s government initially offered differing explanations as public pressure mounted. Some civilian officials said they lacked complete information about military operations. Then-prime minister Abhisit Vejjajiva promised an inquiry and acknowledged that boats had, in some instances, been sent away from Thailand, while saying the government did not have a policy of allowing people to die at sea.

The authorities maintained that any mistreatment would have been contrary to official policy. Critics, however, said the focus on whether there was a written policy failed to address whether units on the ground had carried out dangerous expulsions in practice.

## Survivors describe hunger, thirst and death

The survivors’ testimony presented a markedly different picture from the military’s account.

Men rescued in Indonesian waters said they had first been detained by Thai forces and later placed aboard vessels without adequate means to navigate. Some described having very small daily rations—occasionally only a little rice and water shared among dozens of passengers. Others said supplies ran out entirely.

Several told investigators that fellow passengers became delirious from thirst or collapsed from weakness. Those who died were reportedly thrown into the sea because the survivors had no way to preserve or bury the bodies.

The survivors’ physical condition added weight to calls for an independent investigation. Many arrived severely dehydrated, emaciated or ill. Their condition did not by itself prove who was responsible, given the length and danger of the entire voyage, but humanitarian workers said it was consistent with prolonged deprivation at sea.

Human-rights groups emphasized that these testimonies should not be dismissed simply because the passengers had traveled with smugglers. A person may enter a country irregularly and still be a refugee with a valid claim to protection. Smuggling and asylum are not mutually exclusive, particularly when persecuted people have no legal route to safety.

## Questions of access and accountability

A central dispute was whether independent agencies had been given timely access to all intercepted Rohingya. UNHCR’s ability to interview detainees privately was crucial because refugee screening depends on individual circumstances: where a person came from, why they fled and what danger they would face if returned.

When access is delayed, detainees may be deported or transferred before protection needs are identified. Restricted access also makes allegations of abuse more difficult to verify.

UNHCR and rights organizations called for investigations capable of establishing:

- which Thai units intercepted and detained the boats;
- how many passengers were taken into custody;
- where they were held and for how long;
- whether they were permitted to request asylum;
- whether force was used during detention;
- what condition the boats were in when released;
- how much food, water and fuel was provided; and
- whether commanders authorized or knew about the removal operations.

The controversy highlighted a broader accountability problem in maritime interceptions. Operations often occur far from witnesses, and passengers may disappear into detention, be returned across borders or continue at sea. By the time survivors are found, documentary evidence can be limited and governments may characterize allegations as unverified.

## Thailand’s continuing dilemma

Thailand has long been both a destination and a transit country for displaced people from Myanmar. It hosts large populations from Myanmar along its land border and has frequently provided temporary sanctuary during periods of conflict. At the same time, it has resisted formally recognizing many arrivals as refugees and has often managed them through immigration detention, informal border arrangements or ad hoc humanitarian measures.

Thai officials have argued that the country cannot absorb every irregular arrival and that a unilateral open-door approach could strengthen smugglers. UNHCR has responded that border control and refugee protection are not incompatible. Authorities may investigate trafficking and prosecute smugglers while still rescuing passengers, providing medical care and assessing individual protection claims.

For Rohingya boat people, the absence of regular migration or asylum routes leaves few safe options. Myanmar has denied most of them citizenship and basic rights; Bangladesh hosts a vast refugee population but restricts long-term integration; and other regional states have generally avoided permanent resettlement commitments.

As a result, crackdowns in one country often redirect boats toward another rather than ending the journeys.

## A regional protection failure

The allegations involving Thailand were not an isolated episode. Rohingya boats have also been refused landing or pushed away by other governments in South and Southeast Asia. During later maritime crises, vessels carrying hundreds of people remained at sea while states debated responsibility for their rescue and disembarkation.

UNHCR has repeatedly urged countries in the region to establish coordinated search-and-rescue procedures, guarantee safe disembarkation and share responsibility for screening and shelter. The agency has also called for stronger action against traffickers without criminalizing their victims.

Any durable solution ultimately depends on conditions in Myanmar. Unless Rohingya can obtain citizenship, security and freedom from persecution, people are likely to continue fleeing despite the risks.

## Conflicting narratives, enduring obligations

The dispute over Thailand’s treatment of Rohingya boat people rests on sharply conflicting narratives. Thai military officials have denied deliberately casting migrants adrift and say security forces acted for humanitarian and security purposes. Survivors have described detention, beatings, forced expulsion and days of hunger and thirst on disabled or inadequately supplied boats.

Not every element of those accounts has been independently established, and responsibility for particular deaths is difficult to determine. But the consistency and seriousness of the testimony, together with survivors’ condition when rescued, gave UNHCR substantial grounds to seek access, investigation and safeguards.

The core protection principle is straightforward: irregular entry does not cancel a person’s right to humane treatment, rescue at sea or an opportunity to seek protection from persecution. For UNHCR, Thailand’s legitimate interest in policing its borders cannot justify measures that expose vulnerable people to renewed persecution—or turn the sea itself into a means of expulsion.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on claims that Thai guards whipped Rohingya migrants on a tourist beach and that hundreds later drowned after being towed into open water, using quotes from officials, witnesses, and refugee advocates.
counterfactuals.output:
### Thai forces accused of abusing and abandoning Rohingya at sea

**Bangkok, January 2009** — Thai authorities faced calls for an independent investigation after witnesses said Rohingya migrants were beaten or whipped on an Andaman Sea beach and survivors alleged that security forces later towed boatloads of detainees into international waters and left them without engines or adequate supplies.

Tourists who encountered the detainees described hundreds of men lying in rows under armed guard, some with their hands bound. Witness accounts and photographs appeared to show guards striking migrants with belts or whips. One witness described the men as being treated “like animals,” although access to the detention site was restricted and the precise identities of all the guards could not be independently established.

Survivors who subsequently reached India and Indonesia said Thai forces transferred them to engineless or disabled boats, supplied little food and water, and towed them into the open sea. Some reported that passengers died of dehydration, starvation or drowning during days or weeks adrift. Refugee organizations estimated that several hundred people may have died, but the total could not be independently verified.

Chris Lewa of the **Arakan Project**, which monitors Rohingya migration, said the operation was not an ordinary deportation. “They were put on boats without engines and towed out to sea,” she said, warning that abandoning overcrowded vessels in that condition amounted to putting the passengers’ lives at grave risk.

Thai military officials initially rejected the accusations. Navy commander Admiral Khamthorn Pumhiran said, **“The navy has never pushed them out.”** Other security officials said Thailand had no policy of abandoning migrants and suggested that photographs of the beach detention had been misinterpreted.

Prime Minister Abhisit Vejjajiva later acknowledged that some expulsions may have occurred. **“I have reason to believe that some instances of this happened,”** he told CNN, while saying it remained unclear which officials were responsible. He promised an investigation and said any action taken against migrants should comply with humanitarian standards.

Human Rights Watch and other refugee advocates called for an inquiry independent of the military, access to detainees and an end to forced “push-backs.” They stressed that the Rohingya—many fleeing persecution and statelessness in Myanmar—were entitled to screening for refugee-protection claims and must not be returned or abandoned where their lives were in danger.

The allegations concerned several separate boats and survivor groups, so accounts differed over dates and numbers. Nonetheless, the combination of witness photographs, survivor testimony and the prime minister’s partial acknowledgment intensified scrutiny of Thailand’s treatment of Rohingya arriving by sea.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.output:
**BANGKOK —** Thailand on Tuesday denied allegations that its security forces mistreated refugees from Myanmar or forced boatloads of asylum seekers back into the Andaman Sea, amid renewed scrutiny of operations near the Similan Archipelago.

Government officials said migrants intercepted near **Koh Sai Daeng**, in waters off Thailand’s southwestern coast, had been given food, water and medical assistance before being handled in accordance with immigration law. They rejected accounts alleging that some refugees were beaten, detained on remote islands or placed on unsafe boats and pushed away from Thai territory.

“The Thai government does not have a policy of endangering refugees or violating humanitarian principles,” a government spokesperson said, adding that authorities would investigate credible evidence of misconduct.

Survivors and advocacy groups, however, have alleged changes in Thai government policy that place greater emphasis on intercepting Myanmar refugees at sea and preventing them from landing. They say the approach may amount to an unofficial “pushback” policy, a characterization Thai officials dispute.

Some boats believed to have passed through waters near the Similan Archipelago were later reported near India’s **Andaman Islands** and off **Aceh**, Indonesia, after days at sea. Accounts from passengers could not immediately be independently verified.

The controversy comes as increasing numbers of people flee conflict and persecution in Myanmar, undertaking hazardous journeys across the Andaman Sea. Humanitarian organizations urged Thailand to allow independent monitoring of interception sites and to ensure that asylum seekers are not returned to places where they face persecution.

Thai authorities said the country remained committed to international humanitarian standards but also had a responsibility to combat smuggling networks and protect its maritime borders.

# Thailand accused of pushing Rohingya asylum seekers back to sea

**BANGKOK —** Thailand’s Internal Security Operations Command (ISOC) is facing allegations that security personnel have forced Rohingya asylum seekers back into the Andaman Sea rather than using established overland deportation procedures, raising concerns that those expelled were placed at risk of death.

Survivors and human-rights organizations have alleged that Rohingya arriving by boat were detained on islands or along Thailand’s western coast before being transferred to vessels and towed into international waters. Some accounts say the boats were inadequately supplied with food, water or fuel.

The allegations focus on ISOC, the military-led agency responsible for coordinating internal security operations. Critics say maritime expulsions may have been used to avoid formally deporting the Rohingya through Thailand’s land border with Myanmar, where the predominantly Muslim minority has long faced persecution and restrictions on citizenship and movement.

The claims have not been independently verified in full, and Thai authorities have offered conflicting accounts of how intercepted migrants were handled.

## Navy denies conducting pushbacks

The Royal Thai Navy has denied that it deliberately abandoned Rohingya at sea. Navy officials have said their forces provided humanitarian assistance to boats encountered in Thai waters and maintained that any action involving migrants was conducted under government security policy.

The Navy has also sought to distinguish its role from that of other agencies operating under ISOC’s coordination. Officials rejected accusations that naval personnel had removed boat engines or left passengers without sufficient supplies.

However, survivors’ testimony and reports that military units participated in the interception and transfer of Rohingya boats have intensified calls for an independent investigation and a clear accounting of which agencies issued and carried out the orders.

## UNHCR seeks access

The United Nations refugee agency, UNHCR, expressed concern over the reports and asked Thai authorities for access to detained Rohingya so it could assess whether any had protection needs.

UNHCR emphasized that people seeking asylum should not be returned to places where they face persecution or serious harm. It also warned that pushing overcrowded or unseaworthy boats back to sea without adequate provisions could endanger lives and undermine Thailand’s humanitarian obligations.

Although Thailand is not a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention, it remains bound by other international human-rights standards, including the principle against returning people to situations where they could face torture or other grave abuses.

## Refugees International calls for inquiry

Refugees International said the allegations demanded a transparent investigation and urged Thailand to stop any maritime pushbacks. The advocacy organization called for UNHCR and other independent monitors to be granted access to Rohingya in Thai custody.

The group argued that Rohingya should not be treated simply as illegal migrants because many are fleeing systematic discrimination and statelessness in Myanmar. It also urged regional governments to cooperate on rescue, reception and refugee-status screening rather than forcing boats from one country’s waters into another’s.

Human-rights advocates say an overland deportation would not necessarily be lawful or safe, particularly if it resulted in Rohingya being returned to Myanmar without an assessment of their protection claims. But they stress that sending people out to sea is especially dangerous because it can leave passengers stranded beyond the reach of rescue services.

The controversy has placed renewed scrutiny on Thailand’s treatment of Rohingya arriving by sea and on ISOC’s broad authority over border security. Rights groups say the government must disclose what happened to the intercepted boats, identify the chain of command and ensure that any officials responsible for endangering asylum seekers are held accountable.
